html:
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a draper in Delft who made his own microscopes and became the first person to see and describe single-celled life. He is called the father of microbiology.

His microscopes had a single tiny, carefully ground lens and could magnify about two hundred times or more, better than other instruments of his day. From the 1670s he described tiny animals in pond water, bacteria from his own teeth, sperm cells and red blood cells, in hundreds of letters to the Royal Society in London.

He had no university training and wrote only in Dutch. He was born in the same year and town as Vermeer, and the Scientific Revolution of the Golden Age owes him a whole new world. Nearly two centuries later, germ theory showed what his little animals could do. See the Netherlands.
sum: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a draper in Delft who made his own microscopes and became the first person to see and describe single-celled life. He is called the father of microbiology.
